2801.text: The correct order of dipole moment of the molecules $\mathrm{NH}_3$ (I), $\mathrm{BF}_3$ (II), $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ (III), $\mathrm{NF}_3$ (IV) is
2801.sol:
Dipole moment is a vector quantity. It is defined as the product of the magnitude of the charge and the distance between the centres of the positive and negative charges. Dipole moment of $\mathrm{NF}_3$ and $\mathrm{NH}_3$ The dipole moment of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ is larger than $\mathrm{NF}_3$ because in $\mathrm{NH}_3$, the dipole moment vector of the bond and the lone pairs are in the same direction, while in $\mathrm{NF}_3$, molecule, the dipole moment vector of the lone pair and the bond pairs are opposite in direction.
Dipole moment of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{NH}_3$ They both have dipole moment because they do not have regular geometries. Dipole moment of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is more than $\mathrm{NH}_3$ because $\mathrm{O}$ is more electronegative than $\mathrm{N}$.
Dipole moment of $\mathbf{B F}_3$ It is zero because it has symmetrical (triangular planar) structure.
Therefore, the correct order of dipole moments of molecules is $\mathrm{H}}_{2} \mathrm{O} \text{ (III) }> \mathrm{NH}$}_{3} $\text{ (I) }$>$\mathrm{NF}}_{3} \text{ (IV) }> \mathrm{BF}$}_{3} $\text{ (II) }$

3589.text:
Consider the cell reaction, at 300 K
$\mathrm{A}(s)+\mathrm{B}^{2+}(a q) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A}^{2+}(a q)+\mathrm{B}(s)$
Its $\mathrm{E}^{{}^{\circ}}$ is 1.0 V . The $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{{}^{\circ}}$ of the reaction is $-163 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. What is $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{S}^{{}^{\circ}}$ (in J K${ }^{-1}$ ) of the reaction?
$\left(\mathrm{F}=96500 \mathrm{C} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$
3589.sol:
Given,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{E}^{{}^{\circ}}=1.0 \mathrm{ V} \\
& \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{{}^{\circ}}=-163 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \\
& \mathrm{n}=2 \\
& \mathrm{ T}=300 \mathrm{k} \\
& \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{G}^{{}^{\circ}}=-\mathrm{nFE}{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \\
& =-2 \times 96500 \times 1.0 \\
& =193000 \mathrm{CV} \quad[1 \mathrm{ J}=1 \mathrm{CV}] \\
& =\frac{193000}{1000} \mathrm{ kJ} \quad\left[1 \mathrm{ kJ}=10^3 \mathrm{ J}\right] \\
& \Delta \mathrm{G}^{{}^{\circ}}=193 \mathrm{ kJ} \\
& \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{G}=\Delta \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{T} \Delta \mathrm{ S} \\
& \text{ or, } \Delta \mathrm{S}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{H}-\Delta \mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{ T}} \\
& \Rightarrow \Delta S=\frac{-163+193}{300}=\frac{30}{300}=0.1 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ K}^{-1} \\
& \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{ S}=0.1 \times 10^3 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \\
& \Delta \mathrm{ S}=100 \mathrm{JK}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

Number of stereo isomers& = ${2}^{n}$

Where, $n =$number of stereo centre.

The carbon atom which is attached with four different groups or atoms is known as stereo centre. The $2 -$Bromo$- 3 -$chlorobutane has the two stereo centre. These are represented by the *.

So, the& number of& stereo centre $= n = 2$.

So, the number of stereo isomers =${2}^{2} = 4$

$\left[\because V=288 \pi=\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \Rightarrow 216=r^3 \Rightarrow r=6\right]$

6804.text: Let P be any point on the circle $x^2+y^2=25$. Let L be the chord of contact of P with respect to the circle $x^2+y^2= 9. The locus of the poles of the lines L with respect to the circle $x^2+y^2=36$ is$

Let $P(r, s)$ be point on circle $x^2+y^2=25\mathrm{r}^2+\mathrm{s}^2=25...(i)$
Equation of chord of contact of $P$ w.r.t. circle $x^2+y^2=9$ is L
$\mathrm{L}: \mathrm{xr}+\mathrm{ys}-9=0...(ii)$
Poles of line L w.r.t. circle $x^2+y^2=36$ is ( $h, k$ )
then $\mathrm{xh}+\mathrm{yk}-36=0...(iii)$
Solving (ii) and (iii), we get substitute value of r and s in $e^{\mathrm{n}}$ (i)
$\frac{h}{4}=r, \frac{k}{4}=s \Rightarrow \frac{h^2}{16}+\frac{k^2}{16}=25$
So required locus of pole is $x^2+y^2=400$.

6818.text: The condition that the lines joining the origin to the points of intersection of the line $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=2$ and the circle $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$ are at right angles is
6818.sol:
$\because \frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=2 \Rightarrow \frac{x}{2 a}+\frac{y}{2 b}=1 \begin{aligned}& \&(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r² \\
& \Rightarrow x²+y²-2 a x-2 b y+a²+b²-r²=0
\end{aligned} Homogenizing eqn. (ii), we get \begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow x²+y²-2(a x+b y) 1+\left( a^2+b²-r²\right) 1^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow x²+y²-2(a x+b y)\left(\frac{x}{2 a}+\frac{y}{2 b}\right)+\left( a^2+b²-r²\right) \\
& \left(\frac{x}{2 a}+\frac{y}{2 b}\right)^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 4 a² b²\left( x^2+y²\right)-4 a b(a x+b y)(b x+a y)+ \\
& \left( a^2+b²-r²\right)(b x+a y)^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 4 a² b²\left( x^2+y²\right)-4 a b\left( a b x²+a b y²+\left( a^2+b²\right) x y\right)+ \\
& \left( a^2+b²-r²\right)(b x+a y)^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 4 a² b²\left( x^2+y²\right)-4 a² b²\left( x^2+y²\right)-4 a b \\
& \left( a^2+b²\right) x y+\left( a^2+b²-r²\right)\left( b^2 x²+a² y²\right)+ \\
& \left.\left( a^2+b²-r²\right) 2 a b x y\right)=0
\end{aligned} This is$ the equation of the pair of straight lines joining the origin to the points of intersection of the given lines \& the curve. They will be at right angle if the sum of coefficients of x^2 and y^2$ is zero.
Imposing above condition, we get \begin{aligned}& \left( a^2+b²-r²\right)\left( a^2+b²\right)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow a²+b²-r²=0 \\
& \Rightarrow a²+b²=r²
\end{aligned}
$

7171.text: If the circle $x^2+y^2+2 x+3 y+1=0$ cuts another circle $x^2+y^2+4 x+3 y+2=0$ in $A$ and $B$, then the equation of the circle with $A B$ as a diameter is
7171.sol:
The equation of the circles are
$S_1 \equiv x^2+y^2+2 x+3 y+1=0$ and $S_2 \equiv x^2+y^2+4 x+3 y+2=0$
Since, the circles cuts each other at $A and B$ then equation of $A B$ is
$S_1-S_2=0\Rightarrow \quad\left(x^2+y^2+2 x+3 y+1\right)\Rightarrow \quad-\left(x^2+y^2+4 x+3 y+2\right)=0\Rightarrow \quad-2 x-1=0\Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{-1}{2}$
Putting the value $x=-\frac{1}{2} in S_2$, we get 
$\frac{1}{4}+y^2-2+3 y+2=0\Rightarrow \quad 4 y^2+12 y+1=0\Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{144-16}}{8}\Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{128}}{8}=\frac{-12 \pm 8 \sqrt{2}}{8}\Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{-3}{2} \pm \sqrt{2}$
So intersection points are
$A\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{3}{2}+\sqrt{2}\right) \text{$ and $}\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{3}{2}-\sqrt{2}\right) \text{. }$
Then equation of circle with diameter $A B$ is
$\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)+\left(y+\frac{3}{2}+\sqrt{2}\right)\left(y+\frac{3}{2}-\sqrt{2}\right)=0\Rightarrow \quad\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)^2+\left(y+\frac{3}{2}\right)^2-2=0\Rightarrow x^2+\frac{1}{4}+x+y^2+\frac{9}{4}+3 y-2=0\Rightarrow \quad x^2+y^2+x+3 y+\frac{1}{2}=0\Rightarrow 2 x^2+2 y^2+2 x+6 y+1=0$

Here, $p=\sec ^2 x\Rightarrow \quad \int p d p=\int \sec ^2 x d x=\tan xI F=e^{\tan x}$
Multiplying Eq. (i) by $I F$, we get
$e^{\tan x} \frac{d y}{d x}+e^{\tan x} y \sec ^2 x=e^{\tan x} \cdot \tan x \cdot \sec ^2 x$
Integrating both sides, we get
$y e^{\tan x}=\int e^{\tan x} \tan x \cdot \sec ^2 x d x$
On putting $\tan x=t$,
$\sec ^2 x d x=d t\therefore \quad y e^t=\int t e^t d t=e^t(t-1)+C\therefore \quad y e^{\tan x}=\tan x-1+C e^{-\tan x}$
If $y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1\Rightarrow \quad 1=1-1+C e^{-1} \Rightarrow 1=C e^{-1}\therefore \quad C=e$

15774.subject: Physics
15774.text: The range of a projectile is $100m$. Its kinetic energy will be maximum after covering a distance of:
15774.sol:
The expression for a horizontal range of a projectile is, $R = \dfrac{u^{2}sin\left(2\theta\right)}{g}$ here, $\theta$ is the angle of projection and $u$ is the initial resultant velocity.

The expression for kinetic energy is, $KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

For the maximum kinetic energy, the velocity should be maximum, now the velocity of the projectile is $u = \sqrt{{u}_x^{2} + {u}_y^{2}}$

In the expression of the velocity of particle during projectile, the horizontal component of velocity is constant, i.e., ${u}_{x} = \text{constant}$ therefore, net velocity depends upon the vertical component of velocity, i.e., $u^{2} ∝ {u}_y^{2}\text{or}u^{2}cos\theta$

Therefore, when ${u}_{y}$ is maximum then the net velocity will be maximum and so is the kinetic energy.

Since, ${u}_{y}$ is maximum at the beginning and at the end of the flight of projectile, at the end of the flight of projectile the particle has already covered its horizontal range, therefore, kinetic energy will be maximum after covering a distance of $100m.$

List IList II

options: W - R X - P Y - Q Z - S

Reaction W: Toluene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$) reacts with chromic oxide ($\text{CrO}_3$) in acetic anhydride to form benzylidene diacetate, which on hydrolysis yields benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$). Thus, W matches with R.

Reaction Y: Nitriles ($\text{RCN}$) react with Grignard reagents ($\text{RMgX}$) to form an imine complex, which upon acid hydrolysis yields a ketone ($\text{R}_2\text{CO}$). Thus, Y matches with P.

Reaction Z: Acid chlorides ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$) react with dialkylcadmium ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Cd}$) to form ketones. Here, benzoyl chloride reacts with dimethylcadmium to form acetophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$). Thus, Z matches with Q.

20705.text:
In a closed vessel, 5 moles of $A_2(g)$ and 7 moles of $B_2(g)$ are reacted in following manner.
$A_2(g)+3 B_2(g) \longrightarrow 2 A B_3(g)$
What is the total number of moles of the gases present in the container at the end of the reaction?
20705.sol:
Thus 1 mole of $A_2$ react with 3 mole of $B_2$
$\therefore 7$ moles of $B_2$ will react with $A_2=\frac{7}{3}$ moles
$A_2$ left $=5-\frac{7}{3}=\frac{8}{3}$ moles
1 mole of $A_2$ produces 2 moles of $A B_3$
$\therefore \frac{7}{3}$ moles of $A_2$ will produce $A B_3=\frac{7}{3} \times 2=\frac{14}{3}$ moles
$\therefore$ Total moles of gases in vessel $=\frac{8}{3}$ moles of $A_2+\frac{14}{3}$ moles of $A B_3=\frac{22}{3}$ moles

20784.subject: Chemistry
20784.text: What are the Principal & Azimuthal quantum number values of the valence electrons in tripositive Lutetium?
20784.sol:
The atomic number of Lutetium (Lu) is 71. The electronic configuration of neutral Lutetium is $[Xe] 4f^{14} 5d^{1} 6s^{2}$.

To form the tripositive ion $Lu^{3+}$, three electrons must be removed. The electrons are removed from the outermost shells first, starting with the $6s$ orbital and then the $5d$ orbital.

Removing two electrons from $6s$ and one electron from $5d$ results in the configuration $[Xe] 4f^{14}$.

The valence electrons in $Lu^{3+}$ are the 14 electrons in the $4f$ subshell. For these electrons, the principal quantum number $n$ is 4 and the azimuthal quantum number $l$ for an $f$ orbital is 3.

Answer: $n=4 \quad \ \text{ and } \quad 1=3$

21519.subject: Mathematics
21519.text: The least value of the function $f(x)=a x+\dfrac{b}{x}, \quad(x > 0, b > 0, a > 0)$ is
21519.sol:
The function is given by $f(x) = ax + \dfrac{b}{x}$ for $x > 0$, $a > 0$, and $b > 0$.

Since $ax > 0$ and $\dfrac{b}{x} > 0$, we can apply the Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean (AM-GM) inequality, which states that for positive real numbers $u$ and $v$, $\dfrac{u+v}{2} \ge \sqrt{uv}$.

Let $u = ax$ and $v = \dfrac{b}{x}$. Then,

$\dfrac{ax + \dfrac{b}{x}}{2} \ge \sqrt{ax \cdot \dfrac{b}{x}}$

$\dfrac{f(x)}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}$

$f(x) \ge 2\sqrt{ab}$

The equality holds when $ax = \dfrac{b}{x}$, which implies $x^2 = \dfrac{b}{a}$, or $x = \sqrt{\dfrac{b}{a}}$. Since $x > 0$, this value is valid. Thus, the least value of the function is $2\sqrt{ab}$.

Answer: $2 \sqrt{a b}$

22199.subject: Mathematics
22199.text: The place $x-2 y+z=0$ is parallel to the line
22199.sol:
A line with direction vector $\vec{b} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$ is parallel to a plane with normal vector $\vec{n} = A\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + C\hat{k}$ if and only if $\vec{n} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$.

The normal vector to the plane $x - 2y + z = 0$ is $\vec{n} = 1\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 1\hat{k}$.

We check the dot product for each option:

For (RUsrb), $\vec{b} = 4\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$. $\vec{n} \cdot \vec{b} = (1)(4) + (-2)(5) + (1)(6) = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0$.

Since the dot product is zero, the line is parallel to the plane. We also check if the line lies in the plane by testing a point on the line, such as $(3, 4, 3)$. Substituting into the plane equation: $3 - 2(4) + 3 = 3 - 8 + 3 = -2 \neq 0$. Thus, the line is parallel to the plane and does not lie in it.

Answer: $\dfrac{x-3}{4}=\dfrac{y-4}{5}=\dfrac{z-3}{6}$

22561.subject: Physics
22561.text: Find the current through the 40 $\Omega$ resistor in the given circuit having a diode, three resistors and two cells.
22561.sol:
Let the potential of the common right wire be $0$ V.

Observe the battery symbols to determine their polarities. For the $10$ V battery, the longer line is on the right, so its positive terminal is on the right. For the $5$ V battery, the longer line is on the left, so its positive terminal is on the left.

Therefore, the potential at the node between the $30 \Omega$ resistor and the $10$ V battery is $-10$ V. The potential at the bottom-left node, connected to the positive terminal of the $5$ V battery, is $+5$ V.

Let $V_A$ be the potential at the junction of the $5 \Omega$, $30 \Omega$, and $40 \Omega$ resistors.

Assume the diode is reverse-biased (OFF) so no current flows through the top branch.

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at node $V_A$:

$\dfrac{V_A - (-10)}{30} + \dfrac{V_A - 5}{40} = 0$

$\dfrac{V_A + 10}{30} + \dfrac{V_A - 5}{40} = 0$

Multiplying the equation by $120$ to clear denominators:

$4(V_A + 10) + 3(V_A - 5) = 0$

$4V_A + 40 + 3V_A - 15 = 0$

$7V_A + 25 = 0 \Rightarrow V_A = -\dfrac{25}{7} \text{ V} \approx -3.57 \text{ V}$

The anode is at $V_A = -3.57$ V and the cathode is at $0$ V. Since $V_{anode} < V_{cathode}$, the diode is reverse-biased.

The magnitude of the current through the $40 \Omega$ resistor is:

$I = \dfrac{5 - V_A}{40} = \dfrac{5 - \left(-\dfrac{25}{7}\right)}{40}$

$I = \dfrac{\dfrac{35}{7} + \dfrac{25}{7}}{40} = \dfrac{\dfrac{60}{7}}{40} = \dfrac{60}{280} = \dfrac{3}{14} \text{ A}$

$I \approx 0.214 \text{ A}$

This matches the option $0.21$ A.

23792.text:
Which one of the following choices matches the organs in column I with their vascular system arrangement described in column II?

Column IColumn II
P.Dicot rooti.Radial, open, diarch to tetrarch
Q.Dicot stemii.Ring, conjoint, open
R.Monocot rootiii.Radial, closed, polyarch
S.Monocot stemiv.Scattered, conjoint, closed
23792.sol:
$Dicot root (P) has radial vascular bundles with diarch to hexarch (usually tetrarch) xylem. Secondary growth occurs, so it is considered open. Thus, P matches with (i).

Dicot stem (Q) has conjoint, collateral, and open vascular bundles arranged in a ring. Thus, Q matches with (ii).

Monocot root (R) has radial vascular bundles with polyarch xylem. Secondary growth is absent, so it is closed. Thus, R matches with (iii).

Monocot stem (S) has conjoint, collateral, and closed vascular bundles scattered throughout the ground tissue. Thus, S matches with (iv).

Therefore, the correct matching is P - (i), Q - (ii), \mathbb{R} - (iii), S - (iv).

Answer: P - (i); Q - (ii); \mathbb{R} - (iii); S - (iv)$

26058.subject: Physics
26058.text:
A medium having dielectric constant $K > 1$ fills the space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor. The plates have large area, and the distance between them is $d$. The capacitor is connected to a battery of voltage $V$. as shown in Figure (a). Now, both the plates are moved by a distance of $\dfrac{d}{2}$ from their original positions, as shown in Figure (b).

In the process of going from the configuration depicted in Figure (a) to that in Figure (b), which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
options: The electric field inside the dielectric material is reduced by a factor of $2K$.
The capacitance is decreased by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{K + 1}$.
The voltage between the capacitor plates is increased by a factor of $\left(K + 1\right)$.
The work done in the process DOES NOT depend on the presence of the dielectric material.
26058.sol:
Capacitance of both capacitors are ${C}_{a} = \dfrac{K{ε}_{0}A}{d}$ and ${C}_{b} = \dfrac{{ε}_{0}A}{d + \left(\dfrac{d}{K}\right)} = \dfrac{{ε}_{0}AK}{d\left(K + 1\right)}$

Now, charge stored is ${q}_{a} = \dfrac{K{ε}_{0}A}{d}V$ and ${q}_{b} = \dfrac{{ε}_{0}AKV}{d\left(K + 1\right)}$.

Electric field between each parallel plate capacitor is ${E}_{a} = \dfrac{{q}_{a}}{KA{ε}_{0}} = \dfrac{K{ε}_{0}AV}{dK{ε}_{0}A}$$= \dfrac{V}{d}$ and

${\left({E}_{b}\right)}_{dielectric} = \dfrac{{E}_{air}}{K}$$= \dfrac{{q}_{b}}{KA{ε}_{0}}$$= \dfrac{{ε}_{0}AKV}{d\left(K + 1\right)\left(KA{ε}_{0}\right)}$$= \dfrac{V}{d\left(K + 1\right)}$

So, from above relations, we can see that capacitance decrease by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{K + 1}$.

Work done in the process $W = {U}_{f} - {U}_{i}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left({C}_{f} - {C}_{i}\right){V}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{{ε}_{0}AK}{d\left(K + 1\right)} - \dfrac{K{ε}_{0}A}{d}\right){V}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{V}^{2}\dfrac{{ε}_{0}AK}{d}\left(\dfrac{1}{K + 1} - 1\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{ε}_{0}AK{V}^{2}}{d}\dfrac{1 - K - 1}{K + 1}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{ε}_{0}A{V}^{2}}{d}\left(\dfrac{- {K}^{2}}{K + 1}\right)$

Thus, the work done in the process depends upon the dielectric material.

28112.text:
The value of $K_p$ for the equilibrium reaction $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NO}_2(g)$ is 2 .
The percentage dissociation of $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4(g)$ at a pressure of $0.5 \mathrm{~atm}$ is
28112.sol:
$\begin{array}{llcc} & \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{ g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{ g}) \\ & \text{ Initial moles } & 1 & 0 \\ & \text{ Moles of equil. } & (1-\alpha) & 2 \alpha\end{array}$
(\alpha=$ degree of dissociation $)$
Total number of moles at equil.

\begin{aligned}& =(1-\alpha)+2 \alpha\\
& =(1+\alpha)\\
p_{N_2 \mathrm{O}_{4}} & =\frac{(1-\alpha)}{(1+\alpha)} \timesP\\
p_{N O_2} & =\frac{2 \alpha}{(1+\alpha)} \timesP\\
K_P & =\frac{\left(p_{N_O}\right)^2}{p_{N_2 O_4}}=\frac{\left(\frac{2 \alpha}{(1+\alpha)} \times P\right)^2}{\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}\right) \times P}=\frac{4 \alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}
\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}& \text{ Given, } K_P=2, P=0.5  \mathrm{ atm}\\
& \therefore \quad K_P=\frac{4 \alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}\\
& =\frac{4 \alpha^2 \times 0.5}{1-\alpha^2}\\
& \alpha=0.707 \approx0.71 \\
& \therefore \quad \text{ Percentage dissociation }\\
& =0.71 \times100=71
\end{aligned}
$

For temporary hardness, $Mg{\left({HCO}_{3}\right)}_{2}\overset{\text{heating}}{âŸ¶}Mg{\left(OH\right)}_{2} ↓ + 2{CO}_{2} ↑$

31179.text:
Match List I with List II

List I (Name of polymer) List II (Uses)
A Glyptal I Flexible pipes
B Neoprene II Synthetic wool
C Acrilan III Paints and Lacquers
D LDP IV Gaskets

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :-
options: $A - III, B - II, C - IV, D - I$
$A - III, B - IV, C - II, D - I$
$A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II$
$A - III, B - I, C - IV, D - II$
31179.sol:
(A) Glyptal polymer is used as a manufacture of paints and Lacquers

(B) Neoprene is formed by the free radical polymerisation of chloroprene. It is used for manufacturing conveyor belts, gaskets and hoses.

(C) Polyacrylonitrile is used as a substitute for wool in making commercial fibres as orlon or acrilan.

(D) Low density polythene (LDP) is chemically inert and tough but flexible and a poor conductor of electricity. Hence, it is used in the insulation of electricity carrying wires and manufacture of squeeze bottles, toys and flexible pipes.

From Dalton’s law ${P}_{M} = {y}_{M} \times {P}_{T}$

$\dfrac{{x}_{M}}{{x}_{N}} = \dfrac{{y}_{M}}{{y}_{N}} \times \dfrac{750}{450}$

$\dfrac{{x}_{M}}{{x}_{N}} > \dfrac{{y}_{M}}{{y}_{N}}$

31845.text: Two liquids $X$ and $Y$ form an ideal solution. At $300 \mathrm{~K}$, vapour pressure of the solution containing 1 mol of $X$ and $3 \mathrm{~mol}$ of $Y$ is $550 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}$. At the same temperature, if $1 \mathrm{~mol}$ of $Y$ is further added to this solution, vapour pressure of the solution increases by $10 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}$. Vapour pressure (in $\mathrm{mmHg}$ ) of $X$ and $Y$ in their pure states will be, respectively :

$\begin{aligned}$& P_T=P_X^0 x_X+P_Y^0 x_Y \\
& x_X=$\text{ mol fraction$ of }X \\
& x_Y=$\text{ mol fraction of $}Y \\
& \therefore 550=P_x^{{}^{\circ}}$\left(\frac{1}{1+3}\right)+$P_Y^{{}^{\circ}}$\left(\frac{3}{1+3}\right)$\\
& =$\frac{P_X^0}{4}+\frac{3 P_Y^0}{4}$\\
& \therefore 550(4)=P_X^0+3 P_Y^0
\end{aligned}

Further $1 \mathrm{~mol}$ of Y is added and total pressure increases by $10 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}$.

$\begin{aligned}$& \therefore 550+10=$\mathrm{P}_$X^{{}^{\circ}}$\left(\frac{1}{1+4}\right)+\mathrm{P}_$Y^{{}^{\circ}}$\left(\frac{4}{1+4}\right)$\\
& \therefore 560(5)=$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{X}}^{{}^{\circ}}+$4 $\mathrm{P}_$Y^{{}^{\circ}} \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots(2)
\end{aligned}

By solving (1)$ and (2)
We get,\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{x}}^{{}^{\circ}}=400 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}$
P_Y^{{}^{\circ}}=600 $\mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}$

32047.text: A transition metal $M$ forms a volatile chloride which has a vapour density of $94.8$. If it contains $74.75 \%$ of chlorine the formula of the metal chloride will be
32047.sol:
$74.75 \%$ of chlorine means $74.75 \mathrm{~g}$ chlorine is present in $100 \mathrm{~g}$ of metal chloride.
Weight of metal $=100 \mathrm{~g}-74.75 \mathrm{~g}$ $=25.25 \mathrm{~g}$
Equivalent weight
$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{\text { weight of metal }}{\text { weight of chlorine }} \times 35.5 \\
& =\frac{25.25}{74.75} \times 35.5=12
\end{aligned}
$$
Valency of metal
$$
\begin{array}{r}
=\frac{2 \times \text { V.D. }}{\text { Equivalent wt. of metal }+35.5} \\
=\frac{2 \times 94.8}{12+35.5}=4
\end{array}
$$
$\therefore$ Formula of compound $=\mathrm{MCl}_4$

32526.text:
Consider the reaction
$2\text{H}_2\text{S}(g) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + 2\text{SO}_2(g)$
The magnitude of enthalpy change for the reaction in kJ mol$^{-1}$ is ________. (Nearest integer)
Given: $\Delta_fH^{\ominus}(\text{H}_2\text{S}) = -20.1$ kJ mol$^{-1}$
$\Delta_fH^{\ominus}(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = -286.0$ kJ mol$^{-1}$
$\Delta_fH^{\ominus}(\text{SO}_2) = -297.0$ kJ mol$^{-1}$
32526.sol:
The standard enthalpy of reaction is given by:

$\Delta_r H^{\ominus} = \sum \Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$

For the given reaction:
$2\text{H}_2\text{S}(g) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + 2\text{SO}_2(g)$

$\Delta_r H^{\ominus} = [2 \Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{H}_2\text{O}, l) + 2 \Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{SO}_2, g)] - [2 \Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{H}_2\text{S}, g) + 3 \Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{O}_2, g)]$

Substituting the given values:
$\Delta_r H^{\ominus} = [2(-286.0) + 2(-297.0)] - [2(-20.1) + 3(0)]$

$\Delta_r H^{\ominus} = [-572.0 - 594.0] - [-40.2]$

$\Delta_r H^{\ominus} = -1166.0 + 40.2 = -1125.8 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

The magnitude of the enthalpy change is $1125.8 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $1126$.

Answer: $1126$

33226.sol:
To find point of intersection of two given curves

Put $y = - 2{x}^{2}$ in $y + 3{x}^{2} = 1$

$⇒ {x}^{2} = 1$

$⇒ x = \pm 1$

Let the given equations be ${y}_{1} = 1 - 3{x}^{2}$ and ${y}_{2} = - 2{x}^{2}$.

The desired area would be,

${∫}_{- 1}^{1}\left({y}_{1} - {y}_{2}\right)dx = {∫}_{- 1}^{1}\left(\left(1 - 3{x}^{2}\right) - \left(- 2{x}^{2}\right)\right)dx$

$= {∫}_{- 1}^{1}\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)dx$

$= {\left(x - \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)}_{- 1}^{1} = \left(\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) - \left(- 1 + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)$

$= \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(\dfrac{- 2}{3}\right)$

$= \dfrac{4}{3}sq . units$ .

33899.text: If $Re\left(\dfrac{z - 1}{2z + i}\right) = 1,$ where $z = x + iy,$ then the point $\left(x, y\right)$ lies on a

Let $z = x + iy$
$\left(\dfrac{z - 1}{2z + i}\right) = \dfrac{\left(x - 1\right) + iy}{2\left(x + iy\right) + i} = \dfrac{\left(x - 1\right) + iy}{2x + \left(2y + 1\right)i} \times \dfrac{2x - \left(2y + 1\right)i}{2x - \left(2y + 1\right)i}$
$Re\left(\dfrac{z + 1}{2z + i}\right) = \dfrac{2x\left(x - 1\right) + y\left(2x + 1\right)}{\left(2{x}^{2}\right) + {\left(2y + 1\right)}^{2}} = 1$
$⇒ 2{x}^{2} + 2{y}^{2} - 2x + y = 4{x}^{2} + 4{y}^{2} + 4y + 1$
$⇒ 2{x}^{2} + 2{y}^{2} + 2x + 3y + 1 = 0$
$⇒ {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + x + \dfrac{3}{2}y + \dfrac{1}{2} = 0$

Circle with center $\left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, - \dfrac{3}{4}\right)$
$r = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{9}{16} - \dfrac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4 + 9 - 8}{16}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{4} ⇒ d = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$

where, $d =$diameter of the given circle.

34944.text: If $x^2+y^2+\sin y=4$, then the value of $\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}$ at the point $(-2,0)$ is
34944.sol:
Given, $x^2+y^2+\sin y=4$
After differentiating the above equation $w$.
r. t. $x$ we get

$\begin{aligned}$&2 x+2 y $\frac{d y}{d x}+\cos$y $\frac{d y}{d x}=$0 \ldots(1) \\
&\Rightarrow 2 x+(2 y+\cos y) $\frac{d y}{d x}=$0 \\
&\Rightarrow $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-2 x}{2 y+\cos y}$\\
&$\text{ At }(-$2,0),$\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)_{(-2,0)}=\frac{-2 \times-2}{2 \times 0+\cos 0}$\\
&\Rightarrow$\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)_{(-2,0)}=\frac{4}{0+1}$\\
&\Rightarrow$\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)_{(2,0)}=$4 \ldots(2)
\end{aligned}

Again differentiating equation (1) w. r. t$ to x$, we get
$2+2\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2+2 y \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}-\sin y\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2+\cos \mathrm{y} \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=0\Rightarrow 2+(-2 \sin y)\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2+(2 y+\cos \mathrm{y}) \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=0\Rightarrow(2 y+\cos \mathrm{y}) \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-2-(2-\sin y)\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2\Rightarrow \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=\frac{-2-(2-\sin y)\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2}{2 y+\cos \mathrm{y}}$
So, at $(-2,0)\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=\frac{-2-(2-0) \times 4^2}{2 \times 0+1}\Rightarrow \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=\frac{-2-2 \times 16}{1}\Rightarrow \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-34$

The given information can be represented in the form of a diagram as below:

We need to find the distance $AB$.

Let the distance of $A, B$ from the tower be ${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}$.
$⇒ tan{45}^{°} = \dfrac{5}{{x}_{1}}, tan{30}^{°} = \dfrac{5}{{x}_{2}}$
$⇒ {x}_{1} = 5, {x}_{2} = 5\sqrt{3}$.

$⇒ AB = \sqrt{{{x}_{1}}^{2} + {{x}_{2}}^{2}} = \sqrt{{\left(5\right)}^{2} + {\left(5\sqrt{3}\right)}^{2}} = 10m$

Hence this is the correct option.

37315.text: Let $f ⁡ \left(n\right) = \left[\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{3n}{100}\right]n$, where $[ n ]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $n$. Then $\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{56}f\left(n\right)$ is equal to
37315.sol:
Given $f\left(n\right) = \left[\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{3n}{100}\right]n = \left[\dfrac{9n + 100}{300}\right]n$

If $\dfrac{9n + 100}{300} < 1$

$⇒ 9n + 100 < 300$

$⇒ n < \dfrac{200}{9}$

$⇒ n = 22$

We know that for a number $0 ⩽ x < 1, \left[x\right] = 0$

$⇒ f ( n ) = 0, ∀ 1 ⩽ n ⩽ 22$

Again, if $\dfrac{9n + 100}{300} < 2$

$⇒ 9n + 100 < 600$

$⇒ n = \dfrac{500}{9}$

$⇒ n = 55$

We know that for a number $1 ⩽ x < 2, \left[x\right] = 1$

$⇒ f ( n ) = 1, 23 ⩽ n ⩽ 55$

And, $f ( n ) = 2$ if $n = 56$

Thus, $\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{56}f\left(n\right) = \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{22}0 \times n + \mathop{∑}_{n = 23}^{55}1 \times n + 2 \times 56$

$= 0 + \left(23 + 24 + . . . + 55\right) + 56 \times 2$

$= \dfrac{33}{2}\left(23 + 55\right) + 112$

$= 33 \times 39 + 112$

$= 1399 .$

38359.sol:
Given $2 \cos \theta+\sin \theta=1$
Squaring both sides, we get

$\begin{aligned}&(2 \cos \theta+\sin \theta)^2=1^2 \\
&\Rightarrow 4 \cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta+4 \sin \theta \cos \theta=1 \\
&\Rightarrow 3 \cos ^2 \theta+\left(\cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta\right)+4 \sin \theta \cos \theta\\
&=1 \\
&\Rightarrow 3 \cos ^2 \theta+\not \lambda+4 \sin \theta \cos \theta=1 \\
&\Rightarrow 3 \cos ^2 \theta+4 \sin \theta \cos \theta=0 \\
&\Rightarrow \cos \theta(3 \cos \theta+4 \sin \theta)=0 \\
&\Rightarrow 3 \cos \theta+4 \sin \theta=0 \\
&\Rightarrow 3 \cos \theta=-4 \sin \theta\\
&\Rightarrow \frac{-3}{4}=\tan \theta=\sqrt{\sec ^2 \theta-1}=\frac{-3}{4}\\
&\left(\because \tan ^2 \theta=\sqrt{\sec ^2 \theta-1}\right)\\
&\Rightarrow \sec ^2 \theta-1=\left(\frac{-3}{4}\right)^2=\frac{9}{16}\\
&\Rightarrow \sec 2 \theta=\frac{9}{16}+1=\frac{25}{16} \Rightarrow \sec \theta=\frac{5}{4}
\end{aligned}$ or $\cos \theta=\frac{4}{5}$
Now, $\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta=1 \begin{aligned}&\Rightarrow \sin ^2 \theta+\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^2=1 \\
&\sin ^2 \theta+\frac{4}{5}= 1 \Rightarrow \sin ^2 \theta=1-\frac{16}{25}=\frac{9}{25} \\
&\sin \theta=\pm \frac{3}{5}
\end{aligned}$ Taking $\quad \left(\sin \theta=+\frac{3}{5}\right)$ \quad because $\left(\sin \theta=-\frac{3}{5}\right)$ cannot satisfy the given equation.
Therefore; 7 $\cos \theta+6 \sin $\theta
=7 \times $\frac{4}{5}+6 \times \frac{3}{5}=\frac{28}{5}+\frac{18}{5}=\frac{46}{5}$

38798.text: A series LCR circuit consists of $R = 80 Ω$. ${X}_{L} = 100 Ω$, and ${X}_{C} = 40 Ω$. The input voltage is $2500cos\left(100\pit\right)V$. The amplitude of current, in the circuit, is _____  $A$.
38798.sol:
Comparing input voltage with standard expression, $V = {V}_{0}cos\left(\omegat\right)$, we get $\omega = 100\pi$.

Now, impedance $Z = \sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left({X}_{L} - {X}_{C}\right)}^{2}}$

$= \sqrt{{80}^{2} + {\left(100 - 40\right)}^{2}}$

$= 100Ω$

Therefore, peak current

${i}_{0} = \dfrac{{V}_{0}}{Z} = \dfrac{2500}{100}A = 25A$

$⇒ C = \dfrac{1}{3872}F$

Therefore, $x = 3872$.

39095.subject: Physics
39095.text: Consider a circuit consisting of a capacitor ($20\ \mu$F), resistor ($100\ \Omega$) and two identical diodes as shown in figure. The resistance of diode under forward biasing condition is $10\ \Omega$. The time constant of the circuit is $\alpha \times 10^{-3}$ s. The value of $\alpha$ is _____
39095.sol:
From the given circuit diagram, the battery is connected such that its positive terminal is upwards. This means the current will flow in the clockwise direction during the charging of the capacitor.

In the parallel combination of the two diodes, the left diode is pointing downwards (in the direction of the current) and will be forward-biased. The right diode is pointing upwards (opposite to the current) and will be reverse-biased.

The reverse-biased diode offers infinite resistance and acts as an open circuit. The forward-biased diode offers a resistance of $10\ \Omega$.

The total equivalent resistance of the circuit is the sum of the resistor $R$ and the resistance of the forward-biased diode:
$R_{eq} = 100\ \Omega + 10\ \Omega = 110\ \Omega$

The time constant $\tau$ of the $RC$ circuit is given by:
$\tau = R_{eq}C$
$\tau = 110 \times 20 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}$
$\tau = 2200 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s} = 2.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}$

Comparing this with the given time constant $\alpha \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}$, we get:
$\alpha = 2.2$

Answer: $2.2$

40163.text: An insulated copper wire of $100$ turns is wrapped around a wooden cylindrical core of the cross-sectional area $24{cm}^{2}$. The two ends of the wire are connected to a resistor. The total resistance in the circuit is $12Ω$. If an externally applied uniform magnetic field in the core along its axis changes from $1 . 5T$ in one direction to $1 . 5T$ in the opposite direction, the charge flowing through a point in the circuit during the change of magnetic field will be _____ $mC$.
40163.sol:
The induced emf $\left(ε\right)$ in the turns of the coil can be written as

$\begin{cases}ε & = & - \dfrac{d\phi}{dt} \\ & = & iR . . . \left(1\right)\end{cases}$

Simplify equation (1) to obtain the required charge through a point in the circuit.

$\begin{cases}- \dfrac{d\phi}{dt} & = & iR \\ & ⇒ & - \dfrac{1}{R}{∫}_{{\phi}_{1}}^{{\phi}_{2}}d\phi = ∫ idt \\ & ⇒ & q = \dfrac{{\phi}_{1} - {\phi}_{2}}{R} . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

Where, ${\phi}_{1}, {\phi}_{2}$ are the magnetic flux associated with the coil from two ends.

As, $\phi = NBA$, from equation (2), it can be written that

$q = \dfrac{NA}{R}\left({B}_{1} - {B}_{2}\right) . . . \left(3\right)$

where, $N,A$ are the number of turns and the cross-sectional area of the core respectively.

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) to calculate the required charge.

$\begin{cases}q & = & \dfrac{100 \times 24 \times {10}^{- 4}{m}^{2} \times \left(1 . 5T - \left(- 1 . 5T\right)\right)}{12Ω} \\ & = & 0 . 06C \times \dfrac{1000mC}{1C} \\ & = & 60mC\end{cases}$

40186.subject: Physics
40186.text: A conducting circular loop is placed in $X - Y$ plane in presence of magnetic field $\overset{\to}{B} = \left(3{t}^{3}\overset{^}{j} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{k}\right)$ in SI unit. If the radius of the loop is $1m$, the induced emf in the loop, at time, $t = 2s$ is $n\piV$. The value of $n$ is _____ .
40186.sol:
By the faraday's law in electromagnetic induction

${ε}_{ind} = - \dfrac{d ϕ}{d t} = - \dfrac{d \left(\overset{\to}{B} \cdot \overset{\to}{A}\right)}{d t}$

Magnetic flux is $ϕ = \overset{\to}{B} \cdot \overset{\to}{A}$$= \left(3{t}^{3}\overset{^}{j} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(\pi{\left(1\right)}^{2}\overset{^}{k}\right)$

So, $ϕ = 3{t}^{2}\pi$

Now, induced emf is ${ε}_{ind} = \left|\dfrac{d ϕ}{d t}\right| = 6t\pi$

At $t = 2, {ε}_{ind} = 6\left(2\right)\pi = 12\piV$.

Thus, the value of $n = 12$.

40310.text: An object is placed in a medium of refractive index $3$. An electromagnetic wave of intensity $6 \times {10}^{8}W{m}^{- 2}$ falls normally on the object and it is absorbed completely. The radiation pressure on the object would be (speed of light in free space $= 3 \times {10}^{8}m{s}^{- 1}$ ):
40310.sol:
The formula to calculate the radiation pressure is given by

$P = \dfrac{I}{v} . . . \left(1\right)$

Also, the velocity of the electromagnetic wave can be expressed as

$\mu = \dfrac{c}{v} . . . \left(2\right)$

Equations (1) and (2) imply that

$\begin{cases}P & = & \dfrac{I \cdot \mu}{c} \\ & = & \dfrac{6 \times {10}^{8} \times 3}{3 \times {10}^{8}} \\ & = & 6N{m}^{- 2}\end{cases}$

41707.subject: Physics
41707.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement - I : Susceptibilities of paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances increase with decrease in temperature.

Statement - II : Diamagnetism is a result of orbital motions of electrons developing magnetic moments opposite to the applied magnetic field.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement - I and Statement - II are true.
Both Statement - I and Statement - II are false.
Statement - I is true but Statement - II is false.
Statement- I is false but Statement - II is true.
41707.sol:
Statement-I is true as susceptibility of ferromagnetic and paramagnetic materials is inversely related to temperature, so it increases with decrease in temperature.

Statement-II is also true as because of orbital motion of electrons, the diamagnetic material is able to oppose external magnetic field. Once an external magnetic field is applied, diamagnetic materials develop an induced magnetic field opposite to this field and thus are repelled by the field.

41864.text: A thin $1m$ long rod has a radius of $5mm$. A force of $50{\text{\pi \times 10}}^{3}N$ is applied at one end to determine its Young's modulus. Assume that the force is exactly known. If the least count in the measurement of all lengths is $0 . 01mm$, which of the following statements is false?
options: The maximum value of $Y$ that can be determined is $2 \times {10}^{14}N{m}^{- 2}$
$\dfrac{∆ Y}{Y}$ gets minimum contribution from the uncertainty in the length.
$\dfrac{∆ Y}{Y}$ gets its maximum contribution from the uncertainty in strain.
The figure of merit is the largest for the length of the rod.
41864.sol:
Given, $l = 1m$, $r = 5 \times 1{0}^{- 3}m$ and $F = 50\text{\pi} \times 1{0}^{3}\text{N}$.

Least count in length is $= 0 . 01mm = 0.01 \times {10}^{- 3}m$
Young's modulus is given by $Y = \dfrac{\dfrac{F}{A}}{\dfrac{∆ l}{l}}$
For, $∆ l \to Min$, $Y \to Max$
$⇒ Y\dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \dfrac{F}{A}$
$Y = \dfrac{50\text{\pi} \times 1{0}^{3}}{\text{\pi} \times {\left(5 \times 1{0}^{- 3}\right)}^{2}} \times \dfrac{l}{\Delta l}$
$Y = \dfrac{50 \times 1{0}^{3}}{25 \times 1{0}^{- 6}} \times \dfrac{1}{\Delta l} ⇒ Y = \dfrac{2 \times 1{0}^{9}}{\Delta l}$
Here $\Delta l$ is unknown so we can not find the $Y$

The change in young’s modulus ratio is $\dfrac{∆ Y}{Y} = 2\dfrac{∆ r}{r} + \dfrac{∆ l}{l}$.

As seen from above, the minimum contribution to change in young’s modulus is given by the uncertainty in the length and the maximum contributing to the uncertainty in young’s modulus is given by uncertainty in radius.

Hence, correct option is $A$.

42659.subject: Physics
42659.text:
A uniform disc of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is free to oscillate about the axis $A$ as shown in the figure. For small oscillations the time period is ______.
($g$ is acceleration due to gravity)
42659.sol:
From the given figure, the axis of rotation is a horizontal line passing through the point $A$ on the edge of the disc. The circular arrow around the axis indicates that the disc oscillates out of its plane, meaning the axis of rotation is a tangent to the disc in its own plane.

The moment of inertia of a uniform disc about its diameter is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{4}MR^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the disc about the given axis of rotation is:
$I = I_{cm} + MR^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{5}{4}MR^2$

The distance from the center of mass of the disc to the axis of rotation is $d = R$.

The time period of a physical pendulum is given by:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{Mgd}}$

Substituting the values of $I$ and $d$:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{5}{4}MR^2}{MgR}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{5R}{4g}}$

Answer: $2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{5R}{4g}}$

47610.subject: Chemistry
47610.text: The rate of reaction increases with rise in temperature because of
options: increase in number of activated molecules
increase in the number of effective collisions
47610.sol:
For a collision to be effective, the colloiding molecules must have energy more than a particular value known as threshold energy. At room temperature most of the reactant molecules have energy less than the threshold value. When temperature is increased, the reactant molecules absorb this energy and their energy becomes equal to or greater than threshold value. This extra amount of energy absorbed by the reacting molecules is known as activation energy.
Activation energy $=$ Threshold energy $-$ Average kinetic energy of the reactants.
Evidently, the rate of reaction increases on rise in temperature, because average kinetic energy of the reactants increases and activation energy decreases. Also, on rise in temperature, the number of molecules having kinetic energy greater than threshold value increases. Thus, the increase in the rate of reaction with increase in temperature in mainly due to increase in number of effective collisions.

51781.text: A box contains coupons labeled $1,2,3$....n. A coupon is picked at random and the number $\mathrm{x}$ is noted. The coupon is put back into the box and a new coupon is picked at random. The new number is $y$. Then the probability that one of the numbers $\mathrm{x}$, y divides the other is (in the options below [r] denotes the largest integer less than or equal to $\mathrm{r}$ )
51781.sol:
Let $x=1$
favourable out comes $(1,1),(1,2) \ldots \ldots(1, n)$ no. of favourable out comes when $x=1$
$$
=\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{1}\right]
$$
$\therefore$ no. of favourable out comes when $x=1$ or $y=1$
$$
=2\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{1}\right]-1
$$
no. of favourable out comes when $x=2$ or $y=2$ but $x \neq 1, y \neq 1$
$$
2\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}\right]-1
$$
Similarly
no. of favourable out comes when $x=k$ or $y=k$ but $x, y \notin\{1,2, \ldots . . k-1\}$
$$
2\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{\mathrm{k}}\right]-1
$$
So probability $=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left[\frac{n}{k}\right]-(1+1 \ldots . . n \text{ times })}{n^{2}}$
$$
=\frac{2}{\mathrm{n}^{2}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{n}\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{\mathrm{k}}\right]-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}}
$$

55466.subject: Chemistry
55466.text: Identify neutral aminoacid from following list represented by three letter symbols.
55466.sol:
Amino acid classification depends on the properties of their side chains. Basic amino acids contain proton-accepting groups, acidic amino acids contain proton-donating carboxyl groups, and neutral amino acids lack ionizable groups in their side chains.

Arginine features a guanidinium group that protonates at physiological pH, classifying it as basic. Aspartic acid contains an additional carboxylic acid group, making it acidic. Leucine has a nonpolar aliphatic side chain without ionizable groups, rendering it neutral. Histidine's imidazole ring can accept protons near physiological pH, classifying it as basic.

Among these, only leucine lacks acidic or basic character in its side chain.

55997.text: The rate constant for the reaction $2\text{N}_2\text{O}_5 \rightarrow 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$ is $3.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \texts^{-1}$. If the rate is $2.4 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mole L}^{-1}\ \texts^{-1}$ then the concentration of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5\,(\text{mol L}^{-1})$ is
55997.sol:
From the unit of the rate constant (\texts^{-1}$), we can determine that the given reaction is a first-order reaction.

For a first-order reaction, the rate law is expressed as:
\text{Rate} = k[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]$

Given values are:
$\text{Rate} = 2.4 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mole L}^{-1} \texts^{-1}$
$k = 3.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ s}^{-1}$

Substituting these values into the rate equation:
$2.4 \times 10^{-5} = 3.0 \times 10^{-5} \times [\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]$

Solving for the concentration of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$:
$[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5] = \dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-5}}{3.0 \times 10^{-5}}$

$[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5] = \dfrac{2.4}{3.0}$

$[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5] = 0.8 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$

Answer: $0.8$

57188.subject: Chemistry
57188.text: What is IUPAC name of the following compound?
57188.sol:
To name the cyclic alcohol according to IUPAC rules, the hydroxyl group is prioritized and assigned the lowest possible locant, designating the parent compound as cyclobutanol. The ring must be numbered in the direction that provides the lowest possible locants for the substituents, then ordered alphabetically.

Since the hydroxyl group is fixed at position 1, numbering clockwise places the ethyl group at position 2 and the methyl group at position 4, while counter-clockwise numbering gives the reverse. Both paths yield the locant set $(2,4)$ for the substituents. Alphabetical precedence requires the lower locant to be assigned to the ethyl group, thus the ring is numbered clockwise.

Final name: $2$-$\mathrm{Ethyl}$-$4$-$\mathrm{methylcyclobutanol}$

Comparing with the options, the correct choice is $\boxed{\mathrm{C}}$.

60190.subject: Mathematics
60190.text: The value of $c$ satisfied by the Rolle's theorem for the function $f(x) = x^2(1 - x)^2$, $x \in [0,1]$ is...
60190.sol:
Given function is $f(x) = x^2(1 - x)^2$ on the interval $[0, 1]$.

The function is a polynomial, so it is continuous on $[0, 1]$ and differentiable on $(0, 1)$.

Also, $f(0) = 0$ and $f(1) = 0$, so $f(0) = f(1)$.

By Rolle's theorem, there exists at least one $c \in (0, 1)$ such that $f'(c) = 0$.

Differentiating $f(x)$ with respect to $x$:

$f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}[x^2(1 - x)^2] = 2x(1 - x)^2 + x^2 \cdot 2(1 - x)(-1)$

$f'(x) = 2x(1 - x)[(1 - x) - x] = 2x(1 - x)(1 - 2x)$

Setting $f'(c) = 0$:

$2c(1 - c)(1 - 2c) = 0$

The possible values are $c = 0$, $c = 1$, and $c = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Since $c$ must lie in the open interval $(0, 1)$, the only valid value is $c = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

60560.text: If the area of the region bounded by the parabola $y^2 = 4kx$ and the line $x = k$, (where $k > 0$) is $\dfrac{128}{3}$ sq. units, then the value of $\sin^{-1}  \left(\dfrac{2}{k}\right)is equal to...$

The area of the region bounded by the parabola $y^2 = 4kx$ and the line $x = k$ is given by

$A = 2 \int_{0}^{k} y \, dx$

$A = 2 \int_{0}^{k} \sqrt{4kx} \, dx$

$A = 4\sqrt{k} \left[ \dfrac{2}{3} x^{3/2} \right]_{0}^{k}$

$A = \dfrac{8}{3} k^2$

Given that the area is $\dfrac{128}{3}$, we have

$\dfrac{8}{3} k^2 = \dfrac{128}{3}$

$k^2 = 16$

Since $k > 0$, we get $k = 4$.

Substituting $k = 4$:

$\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{k}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{4}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$

60568.subject: Mathematics
60568.text: The area of the region bounded by the curves $y = |x - 4|$, $x = 3$ and $x = 5$, and the X-axis is
60568.sol:
The required area is given by the definite integral of the function $y = |x - 4|$ from $x = 3$ to $x = 5$.

Area $= \int_{3}^{5} |x - 4| dx$

Since $|x - 4| = -(x - 4)$ for $x < 4$ and $|x - 4| = x - 4$ for $x \geq 4$, we split the integral at $x = 4$:

Area $= \int_{3}^{4} (4 - x) dx + \int_{4}^{5} (x - 4) dx$

Evaluating the first integral:

$\int_{3}^{4} (4 - x) dx = \left[ 4x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{3}^{4} = \left( 16 - \dfrac{16}{2} \right) - \left( 12 - \dfrac{9}{2} \right) = 8 - \dfrac{15}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Evaluating the second integral:

$\int_{4}^{5} (x - 4) dx = \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} - 4x \right]_{4}^{5} = \left( \dfrac{25}{2} - 20 \right) - \left( \dfrac{16}{2} - 16 \right) = -\dfrac{15}{2} - (-8) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Total Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 1$ sq. unit.

Answer: $1$ sq. unit

60921.text:
$\mathrm{f}(x)= \begin{cases}{\left[x^2\right]-\left[-x^2\right],} & x \neq 3 \\ \mathrm{k} & , x=3\end{cases}$

60921.sol:
A function is continuous at a point if the limit exists and equals the function value there. For $f(x)$ defined as $f(x) = \left\{ $\begin{array}{ll} $\left[x^2\right]$ - $\left[-x^2\right]$, & x \neq 3 \\ k, & x = 3 \end{array}$ \right.$, we have $f(3) = k$.

To determine continuity at $x=3$, consider the left-hand limit. As $x \to 3^-$, $x^2 \to 9^-$, so $\left[x^2\right] = 8$ and $\left[-x^2\right] = -9$. Thus, $\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) = 8 - (-9) = 17$.

For the right-hand limit, as $x \to 3^+$, $x^2 \to 9^+$, so $\left[x^2\right] = 9$ and $\left[-x^2\right] = -10$. Therefore, $\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = 9 - (-10) = 19$.

Since the left-hand and right-hand limits are unequal at $x=3$, $\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)$ does not exist. Consequently, no value of $k$ can make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=3$.

Final answer: D

62526.subject: Mathematics
62526.text: For $x > 0$ and $(x \log x) < 1$, if $y = \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x - \log x^{x^2}}{\log e^{x^2} + \log x^x}\right)$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \ldots$
62526.sol:
Given function is:

$y = \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x - \log x^{x^2}}{\log e^{x^2} + \log x^x}\right)$

Simplify the numerator and the denominator of the argument:
Numerator $= x - x^2 \log x = x(1 - x \log x)$
Denominator $= x^2 \log e + x \log x = x^2 + x \log x = x(x + \log x)$

Substitute these back into the function:

$y = \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x(1 - x \log x)}{x(x + \log x)}\right) = \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 - x \log x}{x + \log x}\right)$

We know the inverse trigonometric identity $\cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 - ab}{a + b}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{a + b}{1 - ab}\right)$ (up to a constant multiple of $\pi$ depending on the sign of $a+b$, which becomes zero upon differentiation).

Using $a = x$ and $b = \log x$, and given $x \log x < 1$ (so $1 - ab > 0$):

$y = C + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x + \log x}{1 - x \log x}\right)$

$y = C + \tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1}(\log x)$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan^{-1} x) + \dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan^{-1}(\log x))$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} + \dfrac{1}{1+(\log x)^2} \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(\log x)$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} + \dfrac{1}{x[1+(\log x)^2]}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2} + \dfrac{1}{x[1+(\log x)^2]}$

62834.subject: Mathematics
62834.text: The difference between the maximum value and minimum value of objective function $\mathrm{z}=3 x+5 y$ subject to constraints $x+3 y \leqslant 60$, $x+\mathrm{y} \geqslant 10, x-\mathrm{y}=0, x, \mathrm{y} \geqslant 0$ is
62834.sol:
Feasible region determination
The objective function $z = 3x + 5y$ is subject to constraints: $x + 3y \leq 60$, $x + y \geq 10$, $x = y$, and $x \geq 0$, $y \geq 0$.

Substituting $x = y$ into the inequality constraints yields $4y \leq 60$ and $2y \geq 10$, simplifying to $5 \leq y \leq 15$. With $x = y$, the non-negativity conditions are satisfied. The feasible region is the line segment from $(5,5)$ to $(15,15)$.

Evaluation of objective function
The function values at the endpoints are:
$z(5,5) = 3(5) + 5(5) = 40$
$z(15,15) = 3(15) + 5(15) = 120$

The minimum value is $40$ and the maximum is $120$. The difference is $120 - 40 = 80$.

$\vec{b}_2 = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$

The shortest distance $d$ between two skew lines is given by:
$d = \dfrac{|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$

First, find $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$:
$\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = (\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) - (4\hat{i} - \hat{j}) = -3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k}$

Next, find the cross product $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$:
$\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} \text{ and } \hat{j} \text{ and } \hat{k} \\ 1 \text{ and } 2 \text{ and } -3 \\ 1 \text{ and } 4 \text{ and } -5 \end{vmatrix}$
$\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \hat{i}(-10 + 12) - \hat{j}(-5 + 3) + \hat{k}(4 - 2) = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$

Find the magnitude of $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$:
$|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2| = \sqrt{2^2 + 2^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt{3}$

Now, find the dot product $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)$:
$(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = (-3)(2) + (0)(2) + (2)(2) = -6 + 4 = -2$

Finally, calculate the shortest distance $d$:
$d = \dfrac{|-2|}{2\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

65613.subject: Physics
65613.text: When a capacitor is connected in series LR circuit, the alternating current flowing in the circuit
65613.sol:
The impedance of a series LR circuit is given by $Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$.

When a capacitor is connected in series with the LR circuit, it becomes an LCR circuit. The new impedance is given by $Z_2 = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

The net reactance of the circuit changes from $X_L$ to $|X_L - X_C|$. Since the capacitive reactance $X_C$ opposes the inductive reactance $X_L$, the net reactance generally decreases.

As a result, the overall impedance of the circuit decreases ($Z_2 \lt Z_1$).

Since the alternating current is inversely proportional to the impedance ($I = \dfrac{V}{Z}$), a decrease in impedance leads to an increase in the current flowing through the circuit.

Answer: increases

67671.subject: Physics
67671.text: A wire of length $L$ is bent in the form of a circular coil and current '$i$' is passed through it. This coil is kept in magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil will be maximum, when the number of turns is ___
67671.sol:
The torque acting on a circular coil of $N$ turns in a magnetic field is given by $\tau = N i A B \sin \theta$.

For maximum torque, $\sin \theta = 1$, giving $\tau = N i A B$.

Let $r$ be the radius of the coil. The total length of the wire is $L = N(2 \pi r)$, which gives $r = \dfrac{L}{2 \pi N}$.

The area of the coil is $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \left( \dfrac{L}{2 \pi N} \right)^2 = \dfrac{L^2}{4 \pi N^2}$.

Substituting the area into the torque expression, we get $\tau = N i \left( \dfrac{L^2}{4 \pi N^2} \right) B = \dfrac{i L^2 B}{4 \pi N}$.

For the torque to be maximum, the number of turns $N$ must be minimum.

Since $N$ is a positive integer, the minimum possible value is $N = 1$.

Answer: $1$

69156.text: A mass tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circular path with a constant angular velocity and its angular momentum is 'L'. If the length of the string is now halved, keeping angular velocity same then the angular momentum will be
69156.sol:
The angular momentum of a particle of mass $m$ moving in a circle of radius $r$ with angular velocity $\omega$ is given by $L = I\omega = mr^2\omega$.

Given that the initial angular momentum is $L = mr^2\omega$.

When the length of the string is halved, the new radius becomes $r' = \dfrac{r}{2}$.

The angular velocity $\omega$ is kept constant.

The new angular momentum is $L' = m(r')^2\omega = m\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)^2\omega = \dfrac{mr^2\omega}{4}$.

Substituting the initial angular momentum, we get $L' = \dfrac{L}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{L}{4}$

69729.subject: Physics
69729.text: A black rectangular surface of area A emits energy E per unit time at $27^{}^{\circ}$ C. If length and breadth is reduced to $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{th}$ of initial value and temperature is raised to $327^{}^{\circ}$ C, then energy emitted per unit time becomes
69729.sol:
According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the energy emitted per unit time by a black body is given by $E = \sigma A T^4$.

Initial temperature $T_1 = 27^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C} = 300\text{ K}$ and initial area $A_1 = A$.

Initial energy emitted per unit time is $E_1 = E = \sigma A (300)^4$.

Final temperature $T_2 = 327^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C} = 600\text{ K}$.

Since length and breadth are reduced to $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of their initial values, the new area is $A_2 = \dfrac{L}{4} \times \dfrac{B}{4} = \dfrac{A}{16}$.

Final energy emitted per unit time is $E_2 = \sigma A_2 T_2^4$.

Taking the ratio of $E_2$ to $E_1$:

$\dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1} \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{E_2}{E} = \dfrac{1}{16} \left(\dfrac{600}{300}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{E_2}{E} = \dfrac{1}{16} \times 2^4 = 1$

$E_2 = E$

Answer: $E$

70159.subject: Physics
70159.text: According to corpuscular theory of light, Which is NOT the property of light?
options: The velocity of light does not change after reflection
Light travels in a straight line
The velocity of light in air is greater than in glass
The velocity of light changes after refraction
70159.sol:
According to Newton's corpuscular theory of light, light consists of tiny, perfectly elastic particles called corpuscles that travel in straight lines.

During reflection, the corpuscles undergo perfectly elastic collisions with the reflecting surface, meaning their speed remains unchanged.

To explain refraction, the theory assumes that corpuscles experience an attractive force when approaching a denser medium. This attractive force increases the normal component of their velocity, leading to the conclusion that the speed of light is greater in a denser medium (like glass) than in a rarer medium (like air).

Therefore, the statement that the velocity of light in air is greater than in glass contradicts the corpuscular theory.

Answer: The velocity of light in air is greater than in glass

70198.subject: Physics
70198.text: $The two coherent sources produce interference with intensity ratio 'b'. In the interference pattern, the ratio \frac{I_{\text{max }}+I_{\text{min }}}{I_{\text{max }}-I_{\text{min }}}$ will be
70198.sol:
Let the intensities of the two coherent sources be $I_1$ and $I_2$ where $\frac{I_1}{I_2} = b$, implying $I_1 = b I_2$. The maximum and minimum interference intensities are $I_{\text\max} = (\sqrt{I_1} + \sqrt{I_2})^2$ and $I_{\text\min} = (\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2})^2$. Substituting $I_1 = b I_2$ gives: $I_{\text\max} = I_2 (\sqrt{b} + 1)^2I_{\text\min} = I_2 (\sqrt{b} - 1)^2$ The sum $I_{\text\max} + I_{\text\min} = I_2[(\sqrt{b} + 1)^2 + (\sqrt{b} - 1)^2] = 2I_2(b + 1)$. The difference $I_{\text\max} - I_{\text\min} = I_2[(\sqrt{b} + 1)^2 - (\sqrt{b} - 1)^2] = 4I_2\sqrt{b}$. The ratio simplifies to: $\frac{I_{\text\max} + I_{\text\min}}{I_{\text\max} - I_{\text\min}} = \frac{2(b + 1)}{4\sqrt{b}} = \frac{b + 1}{2\sqrt{b}}$

This result corresponds to option B.

70508.subject: Physics
70508.text: Two uniform wires of same material are vibrating under the same tension. If the $1^{\text{st }}$ overtone of $1^{\text{st }}$ wire is equal to the $2^{\text{nd }}$ overtone of $2^{\text{nd }}$ wire and radius of $1^{\text{st }}$ wire is twice the radius of $2^{\text{nd }}$ wire, the ratio of length of $1^{\text{st }}$ wire to that $2^{\text{nd }}$ wire is
70508.sol:
The fundamental frequency relationship for a string fixed at both ends gives the $n$th overtone frequency as $f_n = (n+1)\frac{v}{2L}$, where $v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ is the wave speed and $\mu = \rho\pi r^2$ is the mass per unit length for a wire of radius $r$ and density $\rho$.

Substituting yields $f_n = \frac{(n+1)}{2Lr}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$. For the first wire's first overtone ($n=1$), $f_1 = \frac{1}{L_1r_1}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$, and for the second wire's second overtone ($n=2$), $f_2 = \frac{3}{2L_2r_2}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$.

Setting $f_1 = f_2$ and canceling the common factor $\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$ gives $\frac{1}{L_1r_1} = \frac{3}{2L_2r_2}$. Given $r_1 = 2r_2$, substitution yields $\frac{1}{2L_1r_2} = \frac{3}{2L_2r_2}$, which simplifies to $\frac{1}{L_1} = \frac{3}{L_2}$.

The ratio is therefore $L_1:L_2 = 1:3$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

71037.text: Which of the following correctly explains Net Primary Productivity?
options: Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.
Rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis.
Gross primary productivity minus respiratory losses.
Rate of assimilation of food energy by consumers.
71037.sol:
Gross primary productivity (GPP) of an ecosystem is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis.

A considerable amount of GPP is utilised by plants in respiration. Gross primary productivity minus respiratory losses (R), is the net primary productivity (NPP).

NPP = GPP - R

Net primary productivity is the available biomass for the consumption to heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers).

Answer: Gross primary productivity minus respiratory losses.

71038.text:
Given below are two statements regarding ecological succession.
Statement I: There is a change in the diversity of species of organisms.
Statement II: There is an increase in the number of species and organisms.
based on the above statements choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
71038.sol:
Ecological succession is the gradual and fairly predictable change in the species composition of a given area.

During succession, some species colonise an area and their populations become more numerous, whereas populations of other species decline and even disappear.

In the successive seral stages, there is a change in the diversity of species of organisms, an increase in the number of species and organisms, as well as an increase in the total biomass.

Thus, both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

Answer: Both Statement I and statement II are correct.

71087.subject: Biology
71087.text: Reproductive isolation occurs due to all of the following EXCEPT
71087.sol:
Reproductive isolation refers to the intrinsic biological mechanisms (pre-zygotic and post-zygotic barriers) that prevent two populations from interbreeding and producing fertile offspring. These mechanisms include changes in genetic material, structural differences in genital organs (mechanical isolation), and changes in the gene pool that lead to behavioral or temporal isolation.

Barriers such as glaciers, mountains, or rivers cause geographical isolation, which is an extrinsic physical barrier. While geographical isolation can eventually lead to reproductive isolation over time due to independent evolution of the separated populations, it is not a reproductive isolation mechanism itself.

Answer: Barriers like glacier

71449.sol:
Glycolysis is the metabolic pathway that converts glucose into two molecules of pyruvic acid.

It occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and is the first step of both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

Lactic acid, acetaldehyde, and ethanol are products formed during fermentation (anaerobic respiration), which takes place after glycolysis.

Therefore, glycolysis ends in the formation of pyruvic acid.

(A). Epidermis.
(B). Middle layers.
(C). Tapetum.
(D). Endothecium.
From the options given below, choose the correct sequence of these layers from inside out.
71487.sol:
The anther wall in angiosperms consists of four layers. From the outermost to the innermost, these layers are the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, and tapetum.

The question asks for the sequence from inside out. Therefore, the innermost layer comes first, followed by the outer layers in order.

The sequence from inside out is:
1. Tapetum (C)
2. Middle layers (B)
3. Endothecium (D)
4. Epidermis (A)

72137.subject: Physics
72137.text: Let '$A$' be the cross-sectional area and '$\rho$' be the specific resistance of a potentiometer wire. If '$I$' is the current passing through the wire, then the potential gradient along the length of the wire is
72137.sol:
Potential gradient is defined as the potential drop per unit length of the wire.

Let $V$ be the potential difference across a length $L$ of the wire.

By Ohm's law, $V = IR$

The resistance $R$ of the wire is given by $R = \rho \dfrac{L}{A}$

Substituting the value of $R$, we get $V = I \left(\rho \dfrac{L}{A}\right)$

The potential gradient is $\dfrac{V}{L} = \dfrac{I\rho}{A}$

Answer: $\dfrac{I\rho}{A}$

72365.subject: Physics
72365.text: If the current gain in common-base configuration (\alpha$) of a transistor increases from 0.95 to 0.96, the percentage change in current gain in common-emitter configuration (\beta$) is approximately
72365.sol:
The relation between common-emitter current gain $\beta$ and common-base current gain $\alpha$ is given by $\beta = \dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}$.

For the initial state, $\alpha_1 = 0.95$.

$\beta_1 = \dfrac{0.95}{1 - 0.95} = \dfrac{0.95}{0.05} = 19$

For the final state, $\alpha_2 = 0.96$.

$\beta_2 = \dfrac{0.96}{1 - 0.96} = \dfrac{0.96}{0.04} = 24$

The change in current gain is $\Delta\beta = \beta_2 - \beta_1 = 24 - 19 = 5$.

The percentage change in $\beta$ is $\dfrac{\Delta\beta}{\beta_1} \times 100 = \dfrac{5}{19} \times 100 \approx 26.31\%$.

Thus, the percentage change is approximately $26\%$.

Answer: $26\%$

72469.subject: Physics
72469.text: In Young's double slit experiment, the intensity on screen at a point, where path difference is '$\lambda/4$', is '$K/4$'. The intensity at a point when path difference is '$\lambda$' will be $[\cos(\pi/4) = 1/\sqrt{2},\ \cos(\pi/2) = 0,\ \cos(2\pi) = 1]$
72469.sol:
The phase difference $\phi$ is related to the path difference $\Delta x$ by the formula:

$\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$

For a path difference of $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$, the phase difference is:

$\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

The intensity $I$ at any point on the screen in Young's double slit experiment is given by:

$I = I_{max} \cos^2 \left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)

Substituting $\phi = $\dfrac{\pi}{2}:

$ I = I_{max} \cos^2$\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) =$ I_{max} $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{I_{max}}{2}

We are given that$ the $intensity at this point is \dfrac{K}{4}. Therefore:

\dfrac{I_{max}}{2} = \dfrac{K}{4} \Rightarrow$ I_{max} = $\dfrac{K}{2}

Now,$ for $a point where the path difference is \Delta$ x = \lambda$, the phase difference is:

$\phi' = $\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \lambda =2\pi

The intensity $ I'$ at this point will be:

$I' = I_{max} \cos^2$\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{2}\right) =$ I_{max} \cos^2($\pi) =$ I_{max} (1)^2 = I_{max}$

Substituting the value of $I_{max}$:

$I' = $\dfrac{K}{2}

Answer: $ K/2

75117.text:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Constitution of India mentions that the Speaker has the power to adjourn both the Houses sine die.
II. On prorogation, it is only the Speaker who can summon the Houses.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
75117.sol:
Statement I is incorrect because the Speaker is the presiding officer of the Lok Sabha and has the power to adjourn only the Lok Sabha sine die. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha has the power to adjourn the Rajya Sabha sine die. The Speaker does not have the power to adjourn both Houses.

Statement II is incorrect because under Article 85(1) of the Constitution of India, it is the President who has the power to summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, not the Speaker.

Therefore, neither Statement I nor Statement II is correct.

Answer: Neither I nor II

78566.text: What is the mean deviation of first 10 even natural numbers?
78566.sol:
First 10 Even Natural numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16,18 and 20.
Mean, $\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x_i}{n}=\frac{2+4+6+\ldots+20}{10}\begin{aligned}
& \bar{x}=\frac{2(1+2+3+\ldots+10)}{10} \\
& \bar{x}=\frac{1}{5} \times \frac{10(10+1)}{2}=11
\end{aligned}\rightarrow$ Now, To calculate Mean deviation, we should calculate $x i-\bar{x}$ for each observation.
$\begin{aligned}
& x i-:-9,-7,-5,-3,-1,1,3,5,7,9 \\
& |x i-|: 9,7,5,3,1,1,3,5,7,9
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Mean deviation, M.D. $=\frac{\sum|x i-\bar{x}|}{n}\begin{aligned}
& \text{ M.D. }=\frac{9+7+5+3+1+1+3+5+7+9}{10} \\
& \text{ M.D. }=\frac{2(1+3+5+7+9)}{10}=\frac{2 \times 25}{10} \\
& \text{ M.D. }=5
\end{aligned}$

84005.subject: Zoology
84005.text: A transgenic food crop, which may help in solving the problem of nightblindness in developing countries is
84005.sol:
Vitamin-A deficiency causes nighthlindness among children. Vitamin-A deficiency often occurs where rice is the staple food since, rice grain does not contain $\beta$ carotene. Three transgenes providing phytoene synthase, phytoene desaturase, zeta carotene desaturase and lycopene cyclase activities were transferred into rice by Agrobacterium mediated transformation. The resulting transgenic rice popularly called Golden rice contains good quantities of $\beta$-carotene.
Flav sav is genetically modified tomato, which remains fresh and retains their flavour much longer than normal tomato due to blocking of synthesis of fruit softening enzyme polygalacturonase.

84350.subject: Zoology
84350.text: Which one of the following experiments suggests that simplest living organisms could not have originated spontaneously from non-living matter?
options: larvae could appear in decaying organic matter
microbes did not appear in stored meat
microbes appeared from unsterilized organic matter
meat was not spoiled, when heated and kept sealed in a vessel.
84350.sol:
The simplest living organisms could not have originated spontaneously from non-living matter. Microbes were killed by heating the meat and the sealed vessel formed a closed system wherein the new microbes could not come in contact with the nutrient medium and hence no spoilage of meat.
Related Theory
Pasteur performed experiments in which he took sterilized yeast and sugar solution in a long necked, then he bent the neck of the flask like a neck of swan. After one month he observed that no life appeared in flask solution because the curved flask neck acts as a filter. He later on broken down the neck and observed the solution. He found that many micro-organisms were originated in solution.

89515.text: In a Bohr's model of an atom, when an electron jumps from n = 1 to n = 3, how much energy will be absorbed?

Energy of an atom when n = 1

${E}_{1} = - \dfrac{1312}{( 1{)}^{2}} = - 1312\text{kJ mo}{\textl^{- 1}$

Similarly energy when $n = 3, \left({E}_{3}\right) = - \dfrac{1312}{( 3{)}^{2}}$

$= - 145.7\text{kJ mo}{\textl^{- 1}$

The energy absorbed when an electron jumps from $n = 1$ to $n = 3$

${E}_{3} - {E}_{1} = - 145.7 - \left(- 1312\right) = 1166.3\text{kJ mo}{\textl^{- 1}$

$= \dfrac{1166.3}{6.023 \times 1{0}^{23}} = 193.6 \times 1{0}^{- 23}kJ$

$= 193.6 \times 1{0}^{- 20}J \left[\text{1 Joule} =1{0}^{7}\text{ergs}\right]

193.6 \times1{0}^{- 13}ergs = 0.1936 \times1{0}^{- 10}ergs$

91525.text: A straight is a five card hand containing consecutive values. If $m$ is equal to the number of ways in which all the five cards, in a straight, are not from the same suit, then the value of $\dfrac{m}{1500}$ is equal to (Consider the value of $J$ as $11, Q$ as $12, K$ as $13$ and Ace as $14$)
91525.sol:
Five consecutive cards can be chosen out of $13$ cards in $9$ ways. $\left(2,3, 4,5, 6\right), \left(3,4, 5,6, 7\right), . . . . . . \left(10, J, Q, K, A\right) .$ The first card can be chosen in $4$ ways (spades, hearts, diamonds and clubs). The second and the subsequent cards, too, can be chosen in $4$ ways.
Thus, there are ${4}^{5}$ ways to choose the five cards.
The number of ways in which all the five cards are not from the same suit is ${4}^{5} - 4 = 1020 .
So, the number of straights in this case is $m = 9 \times 1020 ⇒ $\dfrac{m}{1500} = \dfrac{9 \times 102 0}{150 0} =$6.12

100014.subject: Physics
100014.text:
A student records four measurements of a time interval as $2.3\text{ s}$, $2.4\text{ s}$, $2.6\text{ s}$, and $2.7\text{ s}$. Match the statistical terms in List-I with their corresponding calculated values in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) True value(I) $2.5\text{ s}$
(B) Mean absolute error(II) $0.15\text{ s}$
(C) Fractional error(III) $0.06$
(D) Percentage error(IV) $6\%$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
100014.sol:
First, calculate the true value (mean of the observations):
$T_m = \dfrac{2.3 + 2.4 + 2.6 + 2.7}{4} = \dfrac{10.0}{4} = 2.5\text{ s}$.
So, (A) matches with (I).

Next, find the absolute errors for each measurement:
$\Delta T_1 = |2.3 - 2.5| = 0.2\text{ s}$
$\Delta T_2 = |2.4 - 2.5| = 0.1\text{ s}$
$\Delta T_3 = |2.6 - 2.5| = 0.1\text{ s}$
$\Delta T_4 = |2.7 - 2.5| = 0.2\text{ s}$

Calculate the mean absolute error:
$\Delta T_m = \dfrac{0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2}{4} = \dfrac{0.6}{4} = 0.15\text{ s}$.
So, (B) matches with (II).

Calculate the fractional error:
$\text{Fractional error} = \dfrac{\Delta T_m}{T_m} = \dfrac{0.15}{2.5} = 0.06$.
So, (C) matches with (III).

Calculate the percentage error:
$\text{Percentage error} = \text{Fractional error} \times 100 = 0.06 \times 100 = 6\%$.
So, (D) matches with (IV).

The correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

100499.subject: Physics
100499.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If two particles move in circular paths of different radii with the same uniform linear speed, the particle on the smaller circle experiences a greater centripetal acceleration.
Reason (R): The time period of a particle in uniform circular motion is directly proportional to its radius and inversely proportional to its linear speed.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
100499.sol:
Assertion (A) is true: The centripetal acceleration is given by $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$. For a constant linear speed $v$, $a_c \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$. Thus, a smaller radius $r$ results in a greater centripetal acceleration.

Reason (R) is true: The time period is given by $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$. This shows that $T$ is directly proportional to $r$ and inversely proportional to $v$.

However, Reason (R) does not explain Assertion (A). The correct explanation for the assertion is the inverse relationship between centripetal acceleration and radius for a given speed, not the formula for the time period.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

Assertion A : A spherical body of radius $( 5 \pm 0 . 1 ) mm$ having a particular density is falling through a liquid of constant density. The percentage error in the calculation of its terminal velocity is $4 %$.

Differentiating and dividing by ${V}_{T}$,

So, the percentage error is

As can be seen the terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius. Hence $A$ is true but $R$ is false.

102328.text:
A particle moves such that its position from origin is given by \($\mathrm{x}=$2+3 \sin ^2 $\omega \mathrm{t}$\). Choose CORRECT statement(s) about its motion :-
(A) Particle performs S.H.M. of amplitude \($\frac{3}{2}$m\) and frequency \($\frac{\omega}{\pi}$\)
(B) Particle performs oscillations but no S.H.M.
(C) Particle performs S.H.M. about mean position at \(x=$\frac{7}{2}$m\)
(D) Particle performs oscillations of amplitude 3 m
102328.sol:
1. Analyzing the Statements:
- (A): Particle performs S.H.M. of amplitude \(3, m\) and frequency \($\frac{\omega}{\pi}$\).
- False: The amplitude is actually \($\frac{3}{2},$m\) (not \(3, m\)), and frequency is derived from \(\cos (2 $\omega$t)\) which would be \($\frac{2 \omega}{2 \pi}=\frac{\omega}{\pi}$\), but the amplitude is incorrect.
(B): Particle performs oscillations but no S.H.M.
- False: The particle does perform oscillatory motion about a mean position with a periodic nature (but not simple harmonic due to the \(\sin ^2\) term).
(C): Particle performs S.H.M. about mean position at \(x=7, m\).
- False: The mean position is at \(x=$\frac{7}{2},$m(\operatorname{not} 7, m)\).
(D): Particle performs oscillations of amplitude 3, \(m\).
- False: The amplitude is \($\frac{3}{2},$m\) (not \(3, m\)).

102926.subject: Physics
102926.text: Two solid conducting spheres of radii $R$ and $2R$ are given charges such that their surface charge densities are equal. The ratio of their electric potentials, $V_1 : V_2$, will be:
102926.sol:
The electric potential at the surface of a conducting sphere is $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{r}$.

The charge $Q$ on a sphere can be expressed in terms of its surface charge density $\sigma$ as $Q = \sigma \times 4\pi r^2$.

Substituting this into the potential formula gives:
$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\sigma \times 4\pi r^2}{r} = \dfrac{\sigma r}{\varepsilon_0}$

Since the surface charge density $\sigma$ is the same for both spheres, the electric potential is directly proportional to the radius ($V \propto r$).

Therefore, the ratio of their potentials is:
$\dfrac{V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{R}{2R} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

The ratio is $1 : 2$.

Answer: $1 : 2$

114397.subject: Chemistry
114397.text:
Match List I with List II for an electrochemical cell at $298 \text{ K}$ $\left( \text{Given } \dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059 \text{ V} \right)$:

List I (Cell parameters)List II (Equilibrium constant, $K_c$)
(A) $n=1, E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.118 \text{ V}$(I) $10^2$
(B) $n=2, E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.118 \text{ V}$(II) $10^3$
(C) $n=2, E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.177 \text{ V}$(III) $10^4$
(D) $n=3, E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.059 \text{ V}$(IV) $10^6$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
114397.sol:
The relationship between standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) and equilibrium constant ($K_c$) at $298 \text{ K}$ is given by:
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log K_c$
Rearranging for $\log K_c$ gives:
$\log K_c = \dfrac{n \times E^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{0.059}$

For (A): $\log K_c = \dfrac{1 \times 0.118}{0.059} = 2 \Rightarrow K_c = 10^2$ (Matches I)

For (B): $\log K_c = \dfrac{2 \times 0.118}{0.059} = 4 \Rightarrow K_c = 10^4$ (Matches III)

For (C): $\log K_c = \dfrac{2 \times 0.177}{0.059} = 6 \Rightarrow K_c = 10^6$ (Matches IV)

For (D): $\log K_c = \dfrac{3 \times 0.059}{0.059} = 3 \Rightarrow K_c = 10^3$ (Matches II)

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)

Reason (R) is also true and correctly explains the Assertion. Chemically, almost all enzymes are globular proteins. They have specific shapes and possess active sites on their surface. These active sites have specific geometry where only a substrate molecule with a complementary shape can fit (similar to a lock and key mechanism). This structural complementarity is the reason for their high specificity.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

121771.subject: Botany
121771.text: What is the female sex organ in bryophytes called?
121771.sol: Bryophytes include the various mosses and liverworts that are found commonly growing in moist shaded areas in the hills. Bryophytes are also called amphibians of the plant kingdom because these plants can live in soil but are dependent on water for sexual reproduction. They usually occur in damp, humid and shaded localities. They play an important role in plant succession on bare rocks/soil. The plant body of bryophytes is more differentiated than that of algae. It is thallus-like and prostrate or erect, and attached to the substratum by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids. They lack true roots, stems or leaves. They may possess root-like, leaf-like or stem-like structures. The main plant body of the bryophyte is haploid. It produces gametes, hence is called a gametophyte. The sex organs in bryophytes are multicellular. The male sex organ is called antheridium. They produce biflagellate antherozoids. <mark>The female sex organ called archegonium is flask-shaped and produces a single egg.</mark> The antherozoids are released into water where they come in contact with archegonium. An antherozoid fuses with the egg to produce the zygote. Zygotes do not undergo reduction division immediately. They produce a multicellular body called a sporophyte. The sporophyte is not free-living but attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and derives nourishment from it. Some cells of the sporophyte undergo reduction division (meiosis) to produce haploid spores. These spores germinate to produce gametophyte.
121771.meta: What is the female sex organ in bryophytes called?

123636.subject: Botany
123636.text: What happens to organelles like mitochondria and plastids during cytokinesis in plant cells?
options: They are divided between the two daughter cells
They move to one of the daughter cells
123636.sol: Plant cells however, are enclosed by a relatively inextensible cell wall, thererfore they undergo cytokinesis by a different mechanism. In plant cells, wall formation starts in the centre of the cell and grows outward to meet the existing lateral walls. The formation of the new cell wall begins with the formation of a simple precursor, called the cell-plate that represents the middle lamella between the walls of two adjacent cells. At the time of cytoplasmic division, organelles like mitochondria and plastids get distributed between the two daughter cells. In some organisms karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis as a result of which multinucleate condition arises leading to the formation of syncytium (e.g., liquid endosperm in coconut).
